sources.title: Ralph L. Cohen, Immersions of Manifolds and Homotopy Theory (Harvard CMSA Math-Science Literature Lecture write-up, June 30 2022), complete 46-page author text
sources.locator: §1 “Vector bundle obstructions to embeddings and immersions” (Proposition 1, Theorem 2) and §2.1–2.2 “Foundational work of Whitney, Smale, and Hirsch” (Theorem 4, Theorem 5, the eversion paragraph, Theorem 6), PDF pp. 4–10

contents.name: §1, Proposition 1 and its discussion: the virtual normal bundle obstruction $TM\oplus\nu\cong f^*TN$ and the quotient normal bundle $f^*TN/TM$ of an immersion

§1, Theorem 2 (Hirsch–Smale): a map is homotopic to an immersion iff a virtual normal bundle exists; regular homotopy classes correspond to path components of the bundle-monomorphism space and to isomorphism classes of virtual normals
contents.reason: The cited classification and existence criterion is exactly the predecessor DT-25 page scaffolded as batch 17 of this run; batch 18 consumes that page as its supplier and does not restate or reprove its theorem.

contents.name: §2.1: $\operatorname{Mono}(TM,\mathbb R^{n+k})$ is homotopy equivalent to the space of sections of the fibre bundle $V(TM)\to M$ whose fibres are Stiefel manifolds
§2.1, Theorem 4 (Hirsch–Smale): the derivative map $D:\operatorname{Imm}(M,N)\to\operatorname{Mono}(TM,TN)$ is a weak homotopy equivalence
contents.reason: The weak homotopy equivalence is the DT-25 predecessor's theorem, scaffolded in batch 17 of this run; batch 18 records only the sphere consequences and depends on that page explicitly.

contents.name: §2.1, Theorem 5 (Smale): $\pi_0\operatorname{Imm}(S^n,\mathbb R^{n+k})\cong\pi_n(V_{n,n+k})$ for $k>1$, a surjection for $k=1$, and $V_{n,n+1}\simeq SO(n+1)$
§2.1, eversion paragraph: $SO(3)\cong\mathbb{RP}^3$ with universal cover $S^3$, hence $\pi_2(SO(3))=0$; $\operatorname{Imm}(S^2,\mathbb R^3)$ is path connected and the sphere can be turned inside out
§2.2, Theorem 6: Whitney's embedding theorem in $\mathbb R^{2n}$, uniqueness of embeddings/immersions in high codimension, and Whitney's immersion theorem in $\mathbb R^{2n-1}$
contents.reason: Whitney's high-codimension existence and uniqueness results for arbitrary closed manifolds belong to the later obstruction page of this run; this pair classifies immersions of spheres in minimal codimension only.

contents.name: §3–§4: the immersion conjecture, Massey's characteristic-class bound, Brown–Peterson spaces and Cohen's solution
contents.reason: The immersion conjecture and the $BO/I_n$ Brown–Peterson machinery are higher-codimension characteristic-class theory; the design assigns that material to the later obstruction pair and this pair needs no part of it.

contents.name: §5.2, Theorem 37: Davis' nonimmersion theorem for projective spaces
contents.reason: Davis' nonimmersion theorem is a characteristic-class obstruction result owned by the later obstruction page; this pair only needs one explicit immersion of $\mathbb{RP}^2$, not nonimmersion bounds.

sources.title: John Francis, The h-Principle, Lecture 9: Immersions into Euclidean space, from Smale to Cohen (notes by M. Hoyois), complete 3-page lecture
sources.locator: Corollary 0.1 and the existence criterion; Theorem 0.2 (Whitney); Question 0.3 and Question 0.4; Definitions and Theorems 0.5–0.8 (Wu classes, Massey, Cohen) and Remark 0.9, PDF pp. 1–3

contents.name: Corollary 0.1: $M^n$ immerses in $\mathbb R^{n+k}$ iff a rank-$k$ bundle $V$ with $TM\oplus V\cong\mathbb R^{n+k}$ exists
contents.reason: The existence criterion is a corollary of the DT-25 Smale–Hirsch theorem scaffolded in batch 17; batch 18 uses only the special case of spheres with stably trivial tangent bundle, recorded in its own items.

contents.name: Theorem 0.2 (Whitney): every compact $n$-manifold immerses in $\mathbb R^{2n}$
contents.reason: Whitney's immersion theorem for arbitrary compact manifolds is a high-codimension existence result assigned to the later obstruction page; the sphere case used here is elementary and proved on this page.

contents.name: Questions 0.3–0.4 and Theorems 0.6–0.8: the functions $\beta(n)$, Wu classes, Massey's bound and Cohen's immersion theorem
contents.reason: The immersion-conjecture framework, Wu classes and the Brown–Peterson solution are outside this pair's scope; the design records them for the characteristic-class obstruction development.

contents.name: Remark 0.9: the best linear bound is Whitney's $2n-1$
contents.reason: The optimal high-codimension immersion dimension is a characteristic-class statement not needed for classifying sphere immersions in minimal codimension, and it is not part of this pair's proof route.

sources.title: John Francis, The h-Principle, Lecture 10: Classifying immersions of spheres, after Smale (notes by A. Beaudry), complete 2-page lecture
sources.locator: Definition 0.1 (based immersions and the difference class), Theorem 0.2 (Smale), Corollary 0.3 and its proof, the $n=1$ and $n=2$ computations, and the higher-dimensional discussion, PDF pp. 1–2

contents.name: Definition 0.1: the based immersion space $\operatorname{Imm}_*(S^n,\mathbb R^{n+k})$ as a pullback and the difference class $[f-g]\in\pi_n V_n(\mathbb R^{n+k})$ obtained by gluing the two punctured spheres
Theorem 0.2 (Smale): $\pi_0\operatorname{Imm}_*(S^n,\mathbb R^{n+k})\cong\pi_n V_n(\mathbb R^{n+k})$, a non-canonical isomorphism

Corollary 0.3: for $k>1$, $\pi_0\operatorname{Imm}(S^n,\mathbb R^{n+k})\cong\pi_n V_n(\mathbb R^{n+k})$, proved from the fibre sequence $\operatorname{Imm}_*\to\operatorname{Imm}\to V_n$ and the connectivity of the Stiefel manifold; for $k=1$ the comparison map is a surjection
The fibre sequence $\operatorname{Imm}_*\to\operatorname{Imm}\to V_n(\mathbb R^{n+k})$ and the computations $\pi_0V_n=0$, $\pi_1V_n=0$ for $k>0$ resp. $k>1$

$n=1$, $k=1$: $V_1(\mathbb R^2)$ is homotopy equivalent to $SO(2)$, $\pi_0\operatorname{Imm}(S^1,\mathbb R^2)\cong\mathbb Z$, classified by winding numbers; the circle cannot be turned inside out in the plane
$n=2$, $k=1$: $\pi_2SO(3)=0$, hence $\pi_0\operatorname{Imm}_*(S^2,\mathbb R^3)=0$ and all immersions of $S^2$ in $\mathbb R^3$ are equivalent; the sphere can be turned inside out
The higher-dimensional eversion question: $\pi_0\operatorname{Imm}_*(S^n,\mathbb R^{n+1})\cong\pi_nSO(n+1)$, Bott periodicity and the fibre sequence $SO(n+1)\to SO(n+2)\to S^{n+1}$
contents.reason: The higher-dimensional inside-out question requires the stable homotopy groups of $SO$ and Bott periodicity, which live on the spectra page and are outside this pair's design inventory; only the $S^2$ eversion is in scope.

sources.title: Hassler Whitney, On regular closed curves in the plane, Compositio Mathematica 4 (1937), complete article, pp. 276–284
sources.locator: §1 (regular closed curves, rotation number, invariance under deformation), §2 (Lemma 1 and Theorem 1, the deformation theorem), §3 (normal curves, Lemma 2 and Theorem 2 on double points), pp. 276–284

contents.name: §1: definition of a parametrised regular closed curve; the rotation number as the degree of the unit tangent map; invariance of the rotation number under deformation

§2, Lemma 1 and Theorem 1: the fundamental deformation lemma (prescribed nonvanishing velocity with vanishing average) and the classification: two regular closed curves can be deformed into one another iff their rotation numbers agree
§3, Lemma 2 and Theorem 2: every curve can be made normal by a small deformation, and the rotation number equals the algebraic number of crossings (the 'Umlaufsatz' consequence for simple curves)
contents.reason: The crossing-point formula and generic normality of plane curves are double-point and genericity statements owned by the later embedding-theory pair (DT-27), together with the double-point locus material; the regular-homotopy classification proved here does not use them.

sources.title: Rob Kusner, Conformal geometry and complete minimal surfaces, Bulletin of the AMS (N.S.) 17 (1987), no. 2, complete article, pp. 291–295
sources.locator: Theorem B and Remark 1 (explicit Weierstrass data for the odd-$p$ surfaces $M_p$, immersedness, flat embedded ends), Remark 2–3, Corollary 4 (Boy's surface), pp. 291–295

contents.name: Theorem B and Remark 1: for odd $p\ge3$ the explicit Weierstrass data define an immersed complete minimal surface $M_p\subset\mathbb R^3$ with $p$ flat embedded ends, $M_p\cong\mathbb{RP}^2$ minus $p$ points, and the paper verifies immersedness explicitly from the formula

Corollary 4: Boy's surface is the immersed $\mathbb{RP}^2$ in $\mathbb R^3$ (the compactified $p=3$ surface) achieving the minimal Willmore energy, and every immersed $\mathbb{RP}^2$ in $\mathbb R^3$ has a triple point
Corollary 3 and §3–5: the classification of possible total curvatures and the moduli of static surfaces
contents.reason: The total-curvature spectrum and the moduli of Willmore-minimizing surfaces are minimal-surface theory, not regular homotopy of immersions, and are not part of this pair's scope.

contents.name: The Bryant–Kusner parametrization of Boy's surface and the inversion construction from the minimal immersion of the projective plane with three planar ends; the antipodal identification and the single triple point
Boy's surface as a half-way model for sphere eversion, with the symmetry and animation material
contents.reason: Half-way models and explicit eversion animations are pedagogical, not load-bearing: the eversion theorem on this page is proved by the homotopy-theoretic route through $\pi_2(SO(3))=0$.

contents.name: Chronology: Boy's topological construction, and Apéry's algebraic models
contents.reason: The historical remarks and Apéry's sextic algebraic models are not needed for the immersion example; the parametrization used here is the Bryant–Kusner one.
